body.en: Exploratory data analysis uses graphical and numerical summaries to describe the distribution of one variable and the relationship between two variables. Always describe shape, center, spread, and outliers (S-C-S-O / C-U-S-S) in context using comparative language.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Graphical Displays, Shape, Center, Spread & Linear Transformations

body.en: Distinguish between categorical and quantitative data, construct and interpret dotplots, stemplots, and histograms, describe distribution shape, and determine the exact algebraic impact of linear transformations.

body.en:
When describing or comparing quantitative distributions on the AP exam, you must explicitly state all four characteristics in context with appropriate units:

  • Center: Median or mean with units. Use median for skewed data or datasets with outliers; use mean for approximately symmetric distributions.
  • Unusual Features: Identify any distinct gaps, clusters, or potential outliers.
  • Spread: Interquartile range (IQR), standard deviation, or range with units. Pair median with IQR; pair mean with standard deviation.
  • Shape: Right-skewed (longer right tail: \(\text{mean} > \text{median}\)), left-skewed (longer left tail: \(\text{mean} < \text{median}\)), or approximately symmetric (single unimodal mound, bimodal, uniform).

label.en: ● Theorem — Effects of Linear Transformations on Data: \(y = a + bx\)

body.en:
Suppose every observation \(x_i\) in a dataset is transformed linearly by \(y_i = a + b x_i\):

  • Measures of Center & Position: Shifted by \(a\) AND scaled by \(b\): \[ \bar{y} = a + b\bar{x}, \quad M_y = a + b M_x, \quad Q_{1,y} = a + b Q_{1,x}, \quad Q_{3,y} = a + b Q_{3,x}. \]
  • Measures of Spread: Unaffected by the addition of \(a\); scaled ONLY by \(|b|\): \[ s_y = |b| s_x, \quad \text{IQR}_y = |b| \text{IQR}_x, \quad \text{Range}_y = |b| \text{Range}_x. \]
  • Variance: Multiplied by \(b^2\): \[ s_y^2 = b^2 s_x^2. \]
  • Shape & Outlier Status: Standardized \(z\)-scores and relative shape are preserved. Adding a constant never changes distribution spread or shape.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Unit 1 · Exploring One-Variable & Two-Variable Data)

body.en:
Why Completing the Square & Log-Linearization Work: Any quadratic \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) (\(a \ne 0\)) can be rewritten by factoring \(a\) from the first two terms and adding/subtracting \((b/2a)^2\):

\[ ax^2 + bx + c = a\!\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \left(c - \frac{b^2}{4a}\right) \]

Because \(\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), the extreme value \(k = c - \frac{b^2}{4a}\) is attained uniquely at the axis of symmetry \(x = -\frac{b}{2a}\), restricting the range to \([k, \infty)\) (if \(a > 0\)) and making \(f\) invertible on \(x \ge -\frac{b}{2a}\). Similarly, applying \(\ln\) to power laws \(y = ax^n\) yields \(\ln y = n\ln x + \ln a\), transforming a nonlinear curve into a straight line of gradient \(n\).

A teacher calculates exam scores with mean \(\bar{x} = 68\) and standard deviation \(s = 10\). The teacher applies a curve: \(y = 1.2x + 5\). Find the new mean, standard deviation, and variance of the curved scores.

New Mean: \[ \bar{y} = 1.2(68) + 5 = 81.6 + 5 = \mathbf{86.6\text{ points}}. \]

New Standard Deviation: Adding 5 does not change spread: \[ s_y = |1.2| s_x = 1.2(10) = \mathbf{12.0\text{ points}}. \]

New Variance: \[ s_y^2 = (12.0)^2 = \mathbf{144.0\text{ points}^2}. \]

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — Unit 1 · Exploring One-Variable & Two-Variable Data (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): A histogram is used to display the distribution of the number of hours college students reported spending on social media per day. The bins for the histogram are as follows: 0-2 hours, 2-4 hours, 4-6 hours, 6-8 hours, and 8-10 hours. The heights of the bars are 5, 12, 15, 8, and 3, respectively. What is the total number of students represented by this histogram?

Step-by-Step Solution: The heights of the bars in the histogram represent the frequencies of students in each bin. Summing the frequencies across all five bins gives the total number of students: \[ 5 + 12 + 15 + 8 + 3 = 43. \]

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Unit 1 · Exploring One-Variable & Two-Variable Data)

rows.en: Confuses the product law \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\) with a non-existent sum rule.
Only factor products, quotients, and powers inside logarithms: \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\).
Keeping both roots of \(\sqrt{2x+7} = x - 2\) without checking \(x - 2 \ge 0\)
Squaring both sides loses the sign of \(x - {r}\), introducing roots where \(\sqrt{\cdot} = -\text{number}\).
Enforce the range condition \(x \ge 2\) before or after squaring.
Restricting domain of \(f(x) = (x-3)^2 + 1\) to \(x \ge 0\) for invertibility
The vertex is at \(x = 3\), so \(f(2) = f(4) = 2\) fails the horizontal line test on \(x \ge 0\).
Restrict the domain at the vertex axis of symmetry: \(x \ge 3\) (or \(x \le 3\)).

question.ar:
Level 1 · Foundations

The temperatures (in °C) during a science experiment have median \(M = 22.0^{\circ}\text{C}\) and \(\text{IQR} = 4.5^{\circ}\text{C}\). Convert the temperatures to Fahrenheit باستخدام formula \(F = 1.8C + 32\). What are the median and IQR of the temperatures in °F?

solution.en:
Median in °F: Scaled by 1.8 and shifted by 32: \[ M_F = 1.8(22.0) + 32 = 39.6 + 32 = \mathbf{71.6^{\circ}\text{F}}. \]

IQR in °F: Spread is affected ONLY by the multiplicative factor 1.8, not the addition of 32: \[ \text{IQR}_F = 1.8(\text{IQR}_C) = 1.8(4.5) = \mathbf{8.1^{\circ}\text{F}}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Outlier Identification, Boxplots, Normal Distribution & Pearson's Correlation

body.en: Apply the 1.5 IQR rule for outliers, analyze modified boxplots, calculate standardized normal z-scores, and derive the properties of Pearson's correlation coefficient r.

The Interquartile Range is \(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\), representing the middle 50% of ordered data. Outlier boundaries (fences) are defined by:

\[ \text{Lower Fence} = Q_1 - 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR}, \qquad \text{Upper Fence} = Q_3 + 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR}. \]

An observation is classified as an outlier if it falls strictly below the lower fence or strictly above the upper fence. On a modified boxplot, whiskers extend only to the most extreme non-outlier observations, while individual outliers are plotted as isolated dots or asterisks.

The median and IQR are resistant to extreme values; the mean and standard deviation are non-resistant.

label.en: ● Analytical Definition & Properties of Pearson's Correlation Coefficient \(r\)

body.en:
Pearson's sample correlation coefficient \(r\) quantifies the direction and strength of the linear association between two quantitative variables \(x\) and \(y\):

\[ r = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{s_x}\right)\left(\frac{y_i - \bar{y}}{s_y}\right) = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2}}. \]
  • Bounds: \(-1 \le r \le 1\). \(r = 1\) indicates perfect positive linear association; \(r = -1\) indicates perfect negative linear association; \(r = 0\) indicates no linear association.
  • Unitless & Symmetric: \(r\) has no units and is unchanged if \(x\) and \(y\) are interchanged.
  • Scale & Location Invariance: Transforming \(x\) or \(y\) by \(x' = a + bx\) and \(y' = c + dy\) preserves \(r\) as long as \(b, d > 0\).
  • Linearity Only: \(r\) measures strictly linear relationships; a strong curved pattern (e.g. \(y = x^2\)) can have \(r \approx 0\).
  • Non-resistant: Like the mean, \(r\) is strongly affected by extreme outliers and influential points.

A distribution of salaries has \(Q_1 = \$42,000\) and \(Q_3 = \$68,000\). A director earns \(\$110,000\). Is this salary an outlier according to the 1.5 IQR rule?

Compute IQR: \[ \text{IQR} = 68000 - 42000 = 26000. \]

Upper outlier boundary: \[ Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) = 68000 + 1.5(26000) = 68000 + 39000 = \$107,000. \]

Because \(\$110,000 > \$107,000\), this salary is an outlier.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

The heights of adult males in a region follow a normal distribution with mean \(\mu = 70\) inches and standard deviation \(\sigma = 3\) inches. What is the standardized z-score of a male who is 76 inches tall, and what proportion of adult males are taller than 76 inches?
question.ar:
حل المسألة التالية في (Unit 1 · Exploring One-Variable & Two-Variable Data): Level 2 · Medium

The heights of adult males in a region follow a normal distribution with mean \(\mu = 70\) inches and standard deviation \(\sigma = 3\) inches. What is the standardized z-score of a male who is 76 inches tall, and what proportion of adult males are taller than 76 inches?

solution.en:
Compute the z-score: \[ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{76 - 70}{3} = \frac{6}{3} = \mathbf{2.00}. \]

By the Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7%), approximately 95% of data lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean, leaving 5% split between both tails. The upper tail is: \[ P(Z > 2.00) = \frac{1 - 0.95}{2} = 0.025 = \mathbf{2.5\%} \quad (\text{or } 0.0228 \text{ using exact normal tables}). \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Least-Squares Regression Derivation, Residual Analysis, Outlier Taxonomy & Transformations

body.en: Derive the least-squares regression line (LSRL) by minimizing squared error, interpret slope and intercept in context, evaluate model adequacy via residual plots, diagnose high-leverage and influential points, and linearize non-linear data.

label.en: ● Mathematical Derivation of the Least-Squares Regression Line (LSRL)

body.en:
The Least-Squares Regression Line \(\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x\) minimizes the sum of squared vertical residuals:

\[ S(b_0, b_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - (b_0 + b_1 x_i)\right)^2. \]

Setting the partial derivatives equal to zero:

\[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial b_0} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0 \implies n b_0 + b_1 \sum x_i = \sum y_i \implies b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1 \bar{x}. \]

This proves that the LSRL always passes through the centroid (point of averages) \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\).

Setting \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial b_1} = 0\) and substituting \(b_0\):

\[ b_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = r \frac{s_y}{s_x}. \]

Coefficient of Determination (\(r^2\)): Represents the fraction of total sum of squares explained by the regression:

\[ r^2 = \frac{SSM}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSE}{SST} = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}. \]

Standard Deviation of Residuals: Measures the typical prediction error size in units of \(y\):

\[ s_e = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n - 2}}. \]

label.en: ● Outliers, High-Leverage Points & Influential Points Taxonomy

body.en:
ClassificationDefining CriterionGeometric LocationImpact on Regression Line
OutlierUnusually large residual \(|y_i - \hat{y}_i|\)Far vertically from the regression lineIncreases \(s_e\); weakens correlation \(r\); may shift intercept
High-Leverage PointSubstantially extreme \(x\)-value far from \(\bar{x}\)Far horizontally from the center of \(x\)Has high potential to alter the slope; if it falls along the line, it inflates \(r\)
Influential PointIts removal markedly changes the slope, intercept, or \(r\)Typically an extreme \(x\) point that deviates from the linear trendDrastically tilts the regression line toward itself

• Correlation Does NOT Imply Causation: A high \(r\) or \(r^2\) only demonstrates linear association. Never state that changes in \(x\) cause changes in \(y\) from observational data.
  • Never Extrapolate: Using the LSRL to make predictions for \(x\)-values outside the domain of the original sample data is unreliable and statistically invalid.
  • Interpreting Slope in Context: Always use non-deterministic language: 'For each additional [unit of x], the model predicts an average change of [b₁] in [y]'. Never say 'y increases by b₁'.
  • Sum of Residuals is Always Zero: In any least-squares regression line, \(\sum e_i = \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i) = 0\).
  • Linearizing Data: If a scatterplot is non-linear, transform variables: for exponential growth \(y = a b^x\), graph \(x\) vs \(\ln y\); for power models \(y = a x^b\), graph \(\ln x\) vs \(\ln y\).

A regression model predicting used car price (\(y\), in thousands of dollars) from age (\(x\), in years) yields \(\hat{y} = 28.5 - 2.1x\) with \(r^2 = 0.72\) and \(s_e = 1.8\). A 5-year-old car sells for \(\$16,000\). Calculate the residual, interpret \(r^2\), and interpret \(s_e\) in context.

1. Predicted Price & Residual: \[ \hat{y} = 28.5 - 2.1(5) = 28.5 - 10.5 = 18.0 \implies \$18,000. \] Residual: \[ e = y - \hat{y} = 16.0 - 18.0 = \mathbf{-\$2.0\text{ thousand}} \quad (-\text{\$2,000}). \] The car sold for $2,000 less than predicted by the model.

2. Interpretation of \(r^2 = 0.72\): Exactly 72% of the variation in used car prices is explained by the linear relationship with car age.

3. Interpretation of \(s_e = 1.8\): When using the regression model to predict used car price from age, predictions will typically be off by about $1,800 (1.8 thousand dollars).

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

A scatterplot displays a point at \(x = 18\), where the rest of the sample data has \(x\)-values between 2 and 8. The point falls almost exactly along the linear trend established by the other points. Explain the effect of this point on: (a) leverage, (b) the residual, (c) the correlation coefficient \(r\), and (d) the slope \(b_1\) of the LSRL.
question.ar:
Level 3 · Advanced

A scatterplot displays a point at \(x = 18\), حيث the rest of the sample data has \(x\)-values between 2 and 8. The point falls almost exactly along the linear trend established بتطبيق other points. Explain the effect of this point on: (a) leverage, (b) the residual, (c) the correlation coefficient \(r\), and (d) the slope \(b_1\) of the LSRL.

solution.en:
(a) Leverage: The point has high leverage because its \(x\)-value (18) is substantially far from the mean \(\bar{x}\) of the remaining data.

(b) Residual: The point has a very small residual because it falls directly on the linear trajectory established by the other data points.

(c) Correlation \(r\): Because the point has an extreme \(x\)-value and small residual in line with the trend, it substantially strengthens (increases) the correlation coefficient \(r\) toward 1.

(d) Slope \(b_1\): The point is not influential on the slope; because it already lies on the established trajectory, removing it would cause very little change to the slope \(b_1\).

question.en: [Practice 4 · Easy] A researcher is studying the relationship between study hours and final exam scores for a group of AP Statistics students. The researcher collected data and constructed a scatterplot to visualize the relationship. The scatterplot includes a line of best fit. The equation of the line of best fit is given by \( \hat{y} = 2.5x + 15 \), where \( x \) represents the number of hours studied per week, and \( \hat{y} \) represents the predicted final exam score. If a student studied for \( 12 \) hours, what is the predicted final exam score for that student?
